title: When Does Momentum Help in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards?

paper.title: When Does Momentum Help in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards?
paper.abstract:
Abstract Momentum is a classical tool for accelerating convex optimization and a standard component of modern large language model training.
Yet recent empirical work has questioned the usefulness of first-moment momentum in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR).
We study this question through a bandit formulation of RLVR with bias-corrected exponential moving average (EMA) momentum,
where the EMA coefficient β \beta controls how quickly the weights on past gradients decay. When policy gradients are evaluated exactly,
we prove that increasing β \beta within a range that prevents overshoot strictly accelerates optimization.
When gradients are estimated from sampled responses, a positive expected gain can be obscured by sampling fluctuations.
We show that as the learning rate η \eta decreases, the expected gain with
fixed β \beta vanishes faster than these fluctuations, whereas increasing β \beta to keep η / ( 1 − β ) \eta/(1-\beta) within the safe regime preserves a
nonvanishing gain that eventually dominates them.
Bandit simulations quantitatively validate these predictions.
RLVR experiments on Qwen3-4B-Base using SGD with EMA and AdamW support
our principle of choosing larger coefficients in practical LLM post-training.
On Qwen2.5-32B with AdamW, simply increasing β 1 \beta_{1} improves mean
validation accuracy by nearly 2 2 percentage points over the conventional
choice, demonstrating the principle’s effectiveness at a larger model scale.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become an important approach to improving the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) ( Lambert et al., 2024 ; DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025 ; Yu et al., 2025 ) . In RLVR, responses are sampled from the current policy and evaluated using verifiable rewards, so the training data distribution evolves as the policy changes. This differs from pretraining and supervised fine-tuning, which optimize next-token prediction (NTP) on given text sequences ( Brown et al., 2020 ; Ouyang et al., 2022 ) . Despite these differences, RLVR commonly adopts Adam ( Kingma and Ba, 2015 ) or AdamW ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019 ) , together with conventional first-moment momentum settings ( Zhang et al., 2025 ; Mukherjee et al., 2026 ) . The design and configuration of optimizers for RLVR have received relatively limited attention. One important aspect of optimizer design and configuration is the use of first-moment momentum, implemented in Adam and AdamW as an exponential moving average (EMA) of past gradients. While EMA has shown empirical benefits in NTP training ( Chen et al., 2023 ; Zhao et al., 2025 ) , Mukherjee et al. (2026) report that momentum does not consistently improve performance in their RLVR experiments and can even reduce it under a conventional choice of the momentum coefficient. These observations motivate a closer examination of whether EMA can benefit RLVR and what factors influence its effectiveness. To understand when EMA benefits RLVR and how to choose its coefficient, we adopt a KL-regularized response-level bandit formulation ( Xiong et al., 2024 ) . We analyze natural policy gradient (NPG, Kakade, 2001 ) with a softmax policy parameterization and bias-corrected EMA. NPG provides a tractable theoretical framework for studying policy improvement while controlling changes in the policy distribution, a principle shared by TRPO and PPO ( Schulman et al., 2015 ; Schulman et al., 2017 ; Shani et al., 2020 ) . NPG-based analysis has also provided practical guidance for LLM post-training ( Gai et al., 2026 , e.g., ) . Our contributions are as follows. Deterministic acceleration and stochastic gains. We first prove that, with exact gradients, increasing the EMA coefficient within a safe regime strictly accelerates optimization, which appears to contrast with the limited benefits reported in prior RLVR experiments ( Mukherjee et al., 2026 ) . A deterministic gain, however, need not translate into a consistent improvement when gradients are estimated from sampled responses, as sampling fluctuations may obscure the benefit. We characterize the expectation and variance of the objective gain and prove that, for a fixed EMA coefficient, the expected gain remains positive for sufficiently small learning rates but vanishes faster than the sampling fluctuations as the learning rate decreases (Theorems 4.2 and 5.3 ). Principled selection of momentum coefficients. We next show that scaling the EMA coefficient β \beta with the learning rate η \eta so that η / ( 1 − β ) \eta/(1-\beta) is a positive constant within the safe regime yields a nonvanishing expected gain that eventually dominates sampling fluctuations (Theorem 5.4 ). We further prove that an appropriately increased coefficient allows a smaller learning rate to achieve comparable expected performance under the same update and sample budgets, with asymptotically lower variance of the objective value (Theorem 5.5 ). Validation in bandits and LLM post-training. We quantitatively validate the predicted gain and fluctuation scales in numerical bandit experiments. GRPO experiments ( Shao et al., 2024 ) on Qwen3-4B-Base ( Yang et al., 2025 ) support our theoretical predictions in practical LLM post-training with both SGD with EMA and the widely used AdamW optimizer: larger coefficients improve performance and, when paired with smaller learning rates, yield more stable training with comparable or slightly improved performance. We further demonstrate the principle’s effectiveness at a larger model scale: on Qwen2.5-32B ( Qwen et al., 2024 ) , simply increasing AdamW’s first-moment coefficient improves mean validation accuracy by nearly 2 2 percentage points over the conventional choice.

sections.heading: 2 Related work
sections.text: Optimization and momentum in RLVR. Recent work revisits optimizer design for RLVR through momentum-based normalization ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) , spectral transformations ( Fan et al., 2026 ; Shi et al., 2026 ; Zhu et al., 2026 ) , and parameter-space exploration ( Venkatkrishna et al., 2026 ) . Focusing on optimizer momentum, Fontana et al. (2026) analyze how accumulated AdamW momentum can continue driving updates after clipping suppresses the current policy-gradient contribution during repeated optimization of the same batch. Most directly related to our motivation, Mukherjee et al. (2026) find that SGD can match or outperform AdamW and report no consistent benefit from momentum. Motivated by these empirical findings, we study how the benefit of ordinary EMA momentum in RLVR depends on the momentum coefficient, learning rate, and sampling noise. Momentum in reinforcement learning. Prior work studies momentum for accelerating policy optimization and reducing gradient-estimation error in conventional RL. Chen et al. (2024) establish accelerated convergence for exact-gradient policy optimization under tabular softmax parameterization using Nesterov momentum with a restart rule. Momentum-based variance reduction has also been studied for policy gradient ( Huang et al., 2020 ; Ding et al., 2022 ) and natural policy gradient ( Feng et al., 2024 ) . Huang et al. (2022) develop Bregman policy optimization with basic momentum and a variance-reduced variant. This literature primarily concerns convergence and sample complexity in conventional RL, with reported experiments on control and Atari benchmarks. We study bias-corrected averaging of past natural gradients in a KL-regularized RLVR bandit model, comparing objective values with and without momentum and examining the practical implications through GRPO experiments with language models. Momentum in supervised learning and stochastic optimization. Analyses of online learning and general stochastic optimization characterize regimes in which momentum behaves similarly to SGD under appropriate learning-rate scaling ( Yuan et al., 2016 ; Wang et al., 2024 ) . In language-model pretraining, AdEMAMix combines fast and slow gradient averages to exploit longer gradient memory ( Pagliardini et al., 2025 ) , while ADana combines time-varying momentum schedules with a direct gradient term and damping ( Ferbach et al., 2026 ) . These pretraining studies concern next-token prediction on given text sequences. Our focus is momentum in RLVR, where reward feedback is obtained from responses sampled from the evolving policy.

sections.heading: 6 Experiments
sections.text: We use numerical bandit experiments to quantitatively validate the predictions of Proposition 5.2 and Theorems 5.3 and 5.4 . Then we turn to RLVR experiments on Qwen3-4B-Base to test our theoretical predictions in a practical LLM post-training setting. Finally, we apply our principle of increasing the EMA coefficient to Qwen2.5-32B to assess its applicability as model size increases.

sections.text: We apply the same GRPO setup to Qwen2.5-32B and increase the momentum coefficient in AdamW from 0.9 0.9 to 1 − 10 − 9 1-10^{-9} , using a learning rate of 2 × 10 − 6 2\times 10^{-6} . Simply increasing the momentum coefficient β 1 \beta_{1} substantially improves validation performance. At step 150 150 , the conventional β 1 = 0.9 \beta_{1}=0.9 achieves a mean accuracy of 44.3 % 44.3\% , similar to 44.2 % 44.2\% for the baseline without first-moment momentum, whereas β 1 = 1 − 10 − 9 \beta_{1}=1-10^{-9} reaches 46.1 % 46.1\% , nearly 2 percentage points higher than the conventional setting. Results are shown in Figure 3 .

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: In this work, we explain why momentum’s benefit can be obscured by sampling noise and derive a principle for recovering and exploiting it. We develop a theoretical model and prove that EMA strictly improves the objective value under exact gradients within a range that prevents overshoot. With sampled gradients, fixing β \beta as η \eta decreases makes the expected gain vanish faster than sampling fluctuations, whereas suitably increasing β \beta within the safe regime produces a consistent improvement. GRPO experiments on LLMs confirm the practical benefits of larger momentum coefficients. These findings suggest using coefficients substantially above the conventional β = 0.9 \beta=0.9 to better exploit the first-moment information already maintained by the optimizer.

sections.text: Settings. We use Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen2.5-32B models using the verl training framework. The parameters are set as follows. Parameter Value Parameter Value Training dataset DAPO-17k (English) Generations per prompt 8 Prompts per batch 16 Updates per RL step 1 Max prompt length 2,048 Max response length 4,096 Rollout temperature 1.0 Rollout top- p p 1.0 Clip ratio 0.2 Gradient clipping norm 1.0 KL coefficient 0.01 Training generation seeds 1001, 2001, 3001 Table 2: Shared training settings for the LLM experiments. Prompts and rewards. We use the original prompts provided in the DAPO-17k English dataset. As in DAPO’s implementation, we restrict answer extraction to the final 300 characters of each response. A response receives a reward of 1 1 if the extracted answer matches the ground truth, and 0 0 otherwise. The same rule applies to responses truncated at the length limit; truncation alone does not force a zero reward. Validation. To assess the optimization performance, we evaluate on held-out data drawn from the same distribution as the training data. We construct this validation set by randomly holding out 1,000 problems from the DAPO-17k English dataset and excluding them from training. Evaluation is performed every 20 optimization steps, with an additional evaluation at step 150 for runs ending at that step. For each problem, we sample eight responses at a temperature of 0.7 and top- p p of 1.0, with a maximum response length of 4,096 tokens. Each response receives a binary correctness score from the answer verifier. We report the average score over all 8,000 responses, equivalently the mean per-problem accuracy. All runs use the same held-out problems.
